All right. Good afternoon, everyone. In a short while, I will be joined by a guest, Alexander De Croo, the Administrator of the UN Development Programme. He will join us from Kyiv in Ukraine, where he is currently on a mission. I have the following statement concerning tomorrow's anniversary of the 9/11 attacks. 25 years ago, the heinous terrorist attacks of the 11th of September, 2001, an assault on humanity itself, claimed thousands of lives and left an enduring mark on our world. As we mark this somber occasion on the 11th of September, we remember the nearly 3,000 victims from the United States and more than 90 countries and stand with their families and loved ones. We pay tribute to the survivors and honor the first responders who showed extraordinary courage and humanity in the face of tragedy, many making the ultimate sacrifice. On this solemn anniversary, we stand in solidarity with the people of New York City, the United States of America, and with all those whose lives were affected by the attacks. This year also marks 20 years since Member States adopted the UN Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy, a reminder that the fight against terrorism is a shared, unfinished task. As we pay tribute to the victims, let us renew our shared commitment to build a future free from terrorism. Moving to the situation in Yemen, our colleagues there confirmed that eight UN vehicles were seized from our humanitarian hub in Mocha this morning, amid recent developments in the city. The Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs is deeply concerned by the situation unfolding in the country, stressing that the last thing the people of Yemen need is more fighting and more displacement. These incidents are constraining humanitarian operations and our partners' ability to reach people in need. Communities need an end to the fighting, and humanitarian workers must be able to safely do their jobs. Despite the challenges, rapid response partners have reached more than 2,700 households with emergency assistance. More funding and better access are critical to reach all those who need assistance. Once again, we call on all parties to respect international humanitarian law. They must protect civilians, including by allowing them to move to safer areas, and must facilitate unimpeded access for humanitarian relief to reach all those in dire need. And just to flag that later in the afternoon, the Security Council will hold a session regarding the reported Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia earlier this week. Our Special Envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, will brief. We will share his remarks with you as soon as we get them. Turning to Lebanon, where our peacekeepers of the UN Interim Force continue to observe extensive Israeli Defense Force kinetic activity across the south of the country, including in the airspace, on the ground, and at sea. Yesterday, UNIFIL recorded 84 violations of Lebanese airspace by the IDF, the highest daily number since the 10th of June. Peacekeepers also observed 56 Israeli airstrikes, the highest daily total since the 4th of June. And UNIFIL continues to detect dozens of IDF projectiles impacting targets across southern Lebanon each day. Since the 21st of June, one Hezbollah projectile has been detected, on the 6th of September. Among the most significant observations yesterday was an incident near Al-Mansouri in Sector West, where peacekeepers saw dozens of Israeli drones dropping jerrycans resulting in multiple detonations in the area. At sea, peacekeepers observed two IDF patrol boats violating Lebanese territorial waters off the coast of Nakoura yesterday. Peacekeepers also continue to report unexploded ordnance in both sectors. Recent finds include an explosive shell and a rocket yesterday, as well as a fiber optic drone on Tuesday. And on the humanitarian side, through its Liaison Branch and in coordination with the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, UNIFIL facilitated six humanitarian missions in Sector West yesterday. Turning to the occupied Palestinian territory, the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs warns of the rise in demolitions of Palestinian homes and other properties in the Musafra Yatta area of the southern West Bank in recent days. On Tuesday, Israeli authorities demolished 20 homes and other structures, including a water cistern and solar panels, in two Palestinian herding communities in that area. Combined with the demolition of a third nearby community last Wednesday, these actions have displaced nearly 60 people, half of them children, and otherwise affected 30 people who stay in the area seasonally. Many of the destroyed properties had been built with donor support. Masafi Yatta is home to roughly 1,200 Palestinians living across 13 communities, all under pressure to leave as Israeli authorities have designated this area as a firing zone. Our humanitarian colleagues say that adding to this pressure is a rise in settler violence against those communities, following the establishment of settlement outposts in the area in recent years. Yesterday, the UN and our humanitarian partners visited Masafriyatta to speak with displaced people who are receiving vital assistance, including emergency shelter, food, hygiene, baby products, and psychosocial support. Across the West Bank, 1,500 Palestinians have been displaced so far this year due to demolitions, and more than 2,600 have been displaced due to settler violence and related access restrictions. Turning to the Gaza Strip, yesterday our humanitarian partners visited people who were affected by an airstrike on Al-Bureij area of Deir al-Balah the day before. The UN and our partners are mobilizing rapid support for 30 families who were confirmed to have had their shelters destroyed or damaged. In the first week of September, our humanitarian partners provided rapid assistance to over 100 households affected by 18 incidents reported by communities across the Gaza Strip, including, among others, airstrikes, the collapse of damaged buildings, and domestic fires. Turning to Sudan, the Secretary-General's personal envoy to Sudan, Pekka Haavisto, will conclude his visit to the country on Friday. This week, he joined the quintet the African Union, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, the League of Arab States, the European Union, and the UN on a good offices mission to Khartoum. The quintet held constructive discussions with the chairman and deputy chairman of the Transitional Sovereignty Council, the prime minister, the undersecretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, and other political and civilian actors, including at a working dinner hosted by the Minister of Finance. The mission was focused on listening to Sudanese stakeholders and connecting international efforts with initiatives emerging inside the country. In a statement issued at the conclusion of the mission, the quintet reiterated its commitment to advancing a credible, inclusive, Sudanese-led, and Sudanese-owned political process towards a democratic, civilian-led government that reflects the aspirations of the Sudanese people. Turning to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, our humanitarian colleagues tell us that we and our partners continue to support national authorities in scaling up the response to the Ebola outbreak. Yesterday, a new Ebola treatment center with 50 beds was opened in Kisangani in Tshimpo Province, where new cases continue to be reported. We and our partners are also strengthening disease surveillance and community engagement in areas at heightened risk of transmission. In Ituri Province, BOCHA recently brought together representatives from the mining sector and local authorities to reinforce awareness and disease monitoring in mining communities. Meanwhile, conflict continues to complicate response efforts. Recent armed attacks in Hotweli and Nturi provinces have displaced civilians into Shopo province, raising concerns about the further spread of disease. We reiterate our call for safe and unhindered humanitarian access, as well as sustained international support to help contain the outbreak in DRC and deliver lifesaving assistance for the people in need. Turning to Cuba, our humanitarian colleagues warned that the country's severe power crisis following sanctions is taking an increasing toll on basic services. According to the authorities, electricity generation in August met less than one third of national demand. We are particularly concerned about the impact on healthcare services, including disruptions to critical medical equipment and vaccine cold chain systems, potentially affecting nearly 70,000 children. Humanitarian operations are also facing logistical challenges linked to the over compliance with sanctions, including shipping companies discontinuing services. This is affecting supply chains for medicines, food, water treatment equipment, and other critical supplies across the country. Despite these challenges, we and our partners continue to work closely with authorities to support those with the most severe needs, including hospitalized patients, pregnant women, older people, and children. Since the launch of the Plan of Action last October, humanitarian partners have reached some 1.6 million people with assistance. So far, we have received $42 million of the $94 million required under the Plan of Action, but needs continue to outpace available resources. We reiterate our call on member states to fund the plan of action and facilitate the timely and unimpeded delivery of lifesaving assistance, including fuel for humanitarian purposes. An analysis reached today by the UN Children's Fund shows that more than 171 million students globally, or one in 10 from pre-primary to upper secondary age, had their schooling disrupted by climate hazards in 2025. According to the analysis, storms were the most common cause of school disruptions last year, impacting 109 million students globally. Floods affected at least 70 million students, while heat waves disrupted schooling for approximately 50 million children. UNICEF notes that while students across all income levels were impacted by disruptions, three quarters of students affected live in low and lower middle income countries, where education systems often lack the resources needed to safeguard learning during climate-related emergencies. The report finds that inaction could result in a potential loss of at least $200 billion in lifetime earnings for students who experience climate-related school disruptions in 2025. Thank you. Hello, everyone. I'm standing here in Kyiv. You see the Maidan Square in my back. Second day of visit here in Ukraine. Today, we see that 6.6 million people in Ukraine can have access to electricity because UNDP is assisting them and is rebuilding the energy systems. We are rebuilding the energy systems, but we are especially building them in a better way. We are rebuilding them in a more sustainable way. We are rebuilding them also in a more resilient way. We are moving towards an energy system which is a decentralized system, which in a period of war that we see here, this enables to have a better energy security. And a better energy security is actually linked to security after all. Yesterday, I had the occasion to visit the site of Chernobyl. Chernobyl, which unfortunately is one of the most known places in the world because the biggest human-made, human-caused environmental catastrophe took place there. I've also seen how that structure has been attacked during a drone strike. I want to be very, very clear. Anyone who's attacking those protective structures and those protective structures around a nuclear structure is really gambling with the safety of millions of people. A nuclear installation can never be a target. There can absolutely be no excuse. There can absolutely be no ambiguity. This has to stop. A nuclear structure, and especially a nuclear structure after a nuclear accident, can never be a target of drone attacks. This is something which is unacceptable. And there are plenty of rules that make clear that this can never happen, not even in a situation of war. I would like to end my introduction with an impression. Even in war, there are rules to be followed. These rules came after the Second World War. We have those principles that are there to protect civilians, to protect civilian infrastructure. And we have to be very clear that we condemn these types of attacks. Civilians can never be a military target. Civilian infrastructure can never be a legitimate target of acts of war. There can absolutely be no excuse, there can absolutely be no ambiguity, and there can absolutely be no impunity related to those acts that we have seen here over the past weeks. So this was my introduction, I'm obviously open to answer any questions.
